For graphics cards it generally just comes up to how much you want to spend. Obviously, you can spend loads od money and get a 1080Ti and you will get amazing performance but you could save money and get a 1070 which will net you the majority of the performance but for a much lower price. You have to personally find the place where the increase in cost matches your budget. When you hit high end computer stuff, performance to price doesn't scale linearly. I.E. Core i9 7820X with 8 cores is $599, but 12 core i9 7920X is $1,199. 7920X is twice the price but not twice the cores. The jump from 8 to 10 cores on i9 is even worse, it's a $400 increase for two cores, extra PCIe lanes, and some L3 cache.

You will see the same things with graphics cards, RAM, motherboards (sort of), etc. There always seems to be a curve where things start getting far worse. Regarding i9 series (I use Intel since they like to gouge, not because I like them), the jump from 6 to 8 cores cost $210. The cost from 8 to 10 cores cost $400.

I usually try and find a happy medium. For instance, I bought a Ryzen 1700x (I thought the 1700 would be poorly binned for liquid overclocking and the extra $80 or so would be worth it, I was wrong). I plan on getting a cut down version of the big RX Vega coming out (I'm going to hope I can flash the full RX Vega BIOS to the cut down own and get a full card.

It's all about finding your point where diminishing returns are worth it to you or not. As a general rule, from my experience, the price to performance ratio nosedives after you break the $350 or $400 mark for CPU or graphics card, $200 for motherboard, and $150 for RAM.

This really IS a personal equasion. Personally though, most of my builds have been made not just with "these parts, today" in mind, but also with an upgrade coming in 2-3 years down the road.

I.e. Rather than buying a $300 GPU today, and making it last for 4 years, I can buy a $150 GPU today, and a $150 GPU in 2 years, and squeeze more performance out of my dollar. Not only do I get a technology refresh, where my new card incorporates technologies the old one didn't, but I also get fresh hardware that doesn't have thousands of runtime hours on it. My previous desktop was a Phenom II. It started out in 2010 as an X2 555 that I unlocked into a X4. Then, in 2013, a friend grabbed me a cheap X6 from MicroCenter and I upgraded the RAM, GPU and CPU all at the same time.

If you have a use for multiple computers like me, this is even more helpful. I've got a whole gaming lan built out of salvage from myself and others, due in part to this cyclical upgrade schedule.

I splurged a bit this time, since the Ryzens looked so good, and it had been so long since I built. I'm still planning on an upgrade down the road though.
